source_title: Operation of Unmanned Aircraft System — Definitions — Restrictions (short title "Citizens' Freedom from Unwarranted Surveillance Act" deleted by 2025 amendment)
citation: KRS 500.130 (as amended by 2025 Ky. Acts ch. 19 [HB 19], effective June 27, 2025; originally created 2018 Ky. Acts ch. 26, sec. 1, effective July 14, 2018)
revision_date: 2025-06-27 (2025 Ky. Acts ch. 19); prior version effective 2018-07-14
uas_topic: UAS-facilitated surveillance / privacy; lethal-payload restriction; law-enforcement warrant requirement
regulated_party: Any person operating a UAS (business, recreational, educational, governmental, and law-enforcement operators)
regulated_activity: Operating a UAS for business, recreational, educational, or governmental purposes; conducting a law-enforcement UAS search; recording images of privately owned real property with intent to surveil or publish without consent
requirement_type: Categorical permission for enumerated lawful uses, combined with prohibitions (lethal payload except military; warrantless law-enforcement UAS search; privacy-invasive recording/publication) and a private civil cause of action for the recording prohibition
permit_or_approval_required: No (statute itself does not require a state permit; law enforcement must obtain a UAS-specific warrant to conduct a Fourth Amendment search)
summary: KRS 500.130 authorizes any business entity to operate a UAS for business purposes in compliance with 14 C.F.R. pt. 107, and as of the 2025 amendment expressly lists an entity conducting aerial mapping among the named example business uses (subsection (3)(c)), alongside property appraisers, utilities/communications services, cargo entities, and insurance companies. Recreational use is permitted under 14 C.F.R. pt. 101, and higher-education/school-district UAS use is permitted for educational, research, or testing purposes. UAS may not carry a lethal payload except for specified U.S. military branches. Law enforcement may not use a UAS to conduct a Fourth Amendment search without a warrant that specifically authorizes UAS use, and UAS-derived evidence is generally inadmissible in Kentucky civil, criminal, or administrative proceedings, except as enumerated. A 2025 amendment (HB 19, 2025 Ky. Acts ch. 19) added subsection (12), barring a recreational, business, or educational UAS operator from recording an image of privately owned real property, or a person on it, with intent to surveil or to publish an unauthorized image in violation of a reasonable-expectation-of-privacy presumption keyed to ground-level observability, and created a new private civil cause of action (new sections of KRS Chapters 411 and 413) with a seven-year limitations period. The same 2025 amendment deleted the statute's former short title, the "Citizens' Freedom from Unwarranted Surveillance Act," which had applied to the 2018-2024 version of this section.

source_title: Take of Wildlife with Aircraft Prohibited (Unlawful Use of Aircraft or Unmanned Aircraft)
citation: 301 KAR 3:140, Section 1 (adopted under authority of KRS 150.010(46), 150.025(1), and 150.360; filed with LRC September 9, 2025)
uas_topic: UAS-aided hunting, fishing, and wildlife-harassment restriction (wildlife)
regulated_party: Any person (hunters, anglers, and the general public)
regulated_activity: Using an aircraft or unmanned aircraft system to fish, hunt, or take wildlife; to drive or herd wildlife for those purposes; or to harass wildlife
requirement_type: Prohibition, with enumerated exceptions for department employees/agents, authorized landowners engaged in wildlife damage control, and commercial fishers locating/removing invasive carp
permit_or_approval_required: No standing permit process for the general prohibition; the department-employee and landowner exceptions are status-based, not permit-based
commercial_operator_relevance: Yes — limited to hunting/fishing-related UAS activity, not general commercial UAS use
summary: 301 KAR 3:140, Section 1, effective October 16, 2025, directly names "unmanned aircraft system" in its regulatory text (unlike some other states' agency guidance construing a UAS-silent statute): a person shall not use an aircraft or unmanned aircraft system to fish, hunt, or take wildlife, to drive or herd wildlife for those purposes, or to harass wildlife. Aircraft or UAS may be used by KDFWR employees, contractors, or agents for human safety, law enforcement, research, management, or other department-approved needs; by authorized landowners or their agents for lawful wildlife damage control; and by commercial fishers locating or removing invasive carp. The regulation was adopted under KRS 150.010(46) (department authority to define methods of take), KRS 150.025(1) (authority to regulate methods of take), and KRS 150.360(1) (authority to restrict methods of taking wildlife), following adjournment of the Interim Joint Committee on Natural Resources and Energy on October 16, 2025.

regulated_activity: Operating a UAS into an area a commercial airport's UAS facility map designates as prohibited for UAS operation, takeoff, or landing; operating a UAS recklessly so as to risk serious physical injury or property damage

Subsection (3) expressly exempts a UAS operator engaged in a commercial purpose in compliance with FAA regulations, authorizations, or exemptions from this section's provisions.

citation: KRS 511.100 (created 2018 Ky. Acts ch. 168, sec. 1; amended 2019 Ky. Acts ch. 61, sec. 1; 2020 Ky. Acts ch. 12, sec. 1; 2024 Ky. Acts ch. 167, sec. 1; and most recently 2025 Ky. Acts ch. 42, sec. 1, effective March 19, 2025)
uas_topic: UAS-facilitated critical-infrastructure trespass/surveillance restriction (energy, water, chemical, telecom, rail, food/agricultural facilities, and correctional facilities)
regulated_party: Any person (private and commercial UAS operators and the general public)
regulated_activity: Knowingly using, or authorizing use of, a UAS to fly above real property containing an enumerated 'key infrastructure asset' with intent to cause harm/damage or conduct surveillance, without the property owner's/tenant's/lessee's prior consent; and, for a narrower subset of assets (commercial food-manufacturing and animal-feeding operations), operating a UAS or recording/imaging device above the property, or recording/distributing footage of it, without consent, regardless of intent
requirement_type: Prohibition, with a broad enumerated set of exceptions
permit_or_approval_required: No state permit process; the operative protection is owner/tenant/lessee consent, or falling within an enumerated statutory exception
commercial_operator_relevance: Yes — subsection (4)(d) expressly exempts UAS operation for a commercial purpose in compliance with applicable FAA authorization, regulations, or exemptions from this section
summary: KRS 511.100 defines 15 categories of "key infrastructure asset," including electrical-generation nodes, petroleum refineries, chemical manufacturing/storage facilities, natural-gas and petroleum pipeline facilities, railroad yards/tunnels, drinking-water facilities, state prisons/juvenile-justice facilities/jails and other detention facilities, military-weapons-system facilities, wireless-communications and telecom facilities, commercial food-manufacturing/processing facilities, animal feeding operations, and electrical highway infrastructure. A person commits trespass upon key infrastructure assets (Class B misdemeanor first offense, Class A misdemeanor thereafter) by knowingly using or authorizing use of a UAS to fly above such property with intent to cause harm/damage or conduct surveillance, without the owner's/tenant's/lessee's prior consent (subsection (2)(b)), or, for food-manufacturing and animal-feeding-operation assets specifically, by operating a UAS or recording device above the property, or recording/distributing footage of it, without consent regardless of intent (subsection (2)(c)). Subsection (4) enumerates broad exceptions, including UAS use by the property/asset owner or a person with the owner's lease/permit/authorization; UAS use for a commercial purpose in compliance with applicable FAA authorization, regulations, or exemptions; use by an electric, water, or natural-gas utility company (or a person acting on its behalf) for legitimate business purposes; use by an insurance company for underwriting/damage investigation; use by law enforcement/emergency-management agencies for incident command or related purposes; and use by the federal government, the Commonwealth, or a federal/state contractor.

source_title: Dangerous Contraband (Drones and Unmanned Aircraft) in Detention Facilities — Definitions and Promoting Contraband Offense
citation: KRS 520.010(3) (definitions; amended 2019 Ky. Acts ch. 61, sec. 2, effective June 27, 2019) and KRS 520.050 (Promoting Contraband in the First Degree)
revision_date: 2019-06-27 (most recent amendment adding UAS language to the contraband definition)
uas_topic: UAS as prohibited contraband in correctional/detention facilities (corrections, public safety)
regulated_party: Any person, including persons confined in a detention facility and persons introducing items into one
regulated_activity: Knowingly introducing a drone, unmanned aircraft, other remotely controlled vehicle, or its payload into a detention facility or penitentiary; or, as a confined person, knowingly making, obtaining, or possessing one
commercial_operator_relevance: Yes — relevant to any UAS operator whose flight path or delivery activity could bring a UAS into a detention facility, even inadvertently
summary: KRS 520.010(3) defines "dangerous contraband" for purposes of Kentucky's escape-and-custody offenses to expressly include "drones, unmanned aircraft, or other remotely controlled vehicles, and any payload carried by those vehicles," alongside dangerous instruments, controlled substances, unauthorized cell phones, and metal-cutting tools. This UAS-specific language was added by 2019 Ky. Acts ch. 61, sec. 2 (the same act that, per its companion section 1, amended KRS 511.100's key-infrastructure-asset definition to add correctional facilities, KY-004). KRS 520.050 makes it Promoting Contraband in the First Degree — a Class D felony (Class B felony if the contraband is fentanyl, carfentanil, or a fentanyl derivative) — to knowingly introduce dangerous contraband into a detention facility or penitentiary, or, as a confined person, to knowingly make, obtain, or possess it.

citation: Kentucky Department of Parks "Photo & Drone Policy" webpage (parks.ky.gov) and "Location Contract for Use at State Parks — Unmanned Aerial System (UAS), or Drone" permit form (version January 27, 2026; prior version February 5, 2024)
source_type: Permit or property-use requirement / official agency policy
effective_date: Unknown (current permit form dated 2026-01-27; prior version dated 2024-02-05)
status: Current / in force (as agency permit program, not codified regulation)
uas_topic: State-park/state-land UAS permit requirement (parks, public lands)
regulated_party: Any person seeking to fly a UAS at a Kentucky State Park or Historic Site
regulated_activity: Operating a UAS (recreational or commercial, including for photography/videography) at a Kentucky Department of Parks-managed property
permit_or_approval_required: Yes — a signed Location Contract/drone permit, executed by the Park Manager and Commissioner of Parks (or designee), accompanied by proof of the operator's FAA credential (Remote Pilot Certificate or TRUST certificate) and proof of liability insurance (minimum $1,000,000)
summary: Kentucky's Department of Parks requires a signed "Location Contract for Use at State Parks" permit before any UAS/drone may be flown at a Kentucky State Park or Historic Site, for both recreational and commercial use; the applicant must select the applicable FAA operating rule (49 U.S.C. 44809/Advisory Circular 91-57C recreational or Part 107 commercial), disclose UAS weight class and registration, and specify flight dates/times and, if applicable, photography/filming scope. The applicant must attach a Remote Pilot Certificate or TRUST certificate as applicable and current proof of liability insurance with limits of no less than $1,000,000; commercial/photography use may carry an additional fee determined by the Department. The permit is revocable at the Department's discretion on 24 hours' notice (or without notice if injury or damage is threatened), requires compliance with FAA Rule 107/recreational rules, a no-fly-over-people-without-consent condition, use of the FAA's B4UFLY app before flight, separate USACE/TVA approval where applicable, and an indemnification/hold-harmless clause running to the Commonwealth. Submission of the form alone does not authorize flight; the permit must be executed by the Park Manager and Commissioner of Parks (or designee) before any flight occurs.

uas_topic: State DOT/aviation-office UAS clearinghouse function; federally funded-project UAS procurement/country-of-origin security restriction
regulated_party: KYTC itself, and any "industry partner" (consultant, contractor, or other entity performing federally funded KYTC work, including planning, design, surveying/imagery, construction engineering, and inspection)
regulated_activity: Procuring, operating, or maintaining a UAS (aircraft, flight controller, camera, or ground control station) manufactured by, or subject to the control of, a foreign-adversary country (specifically identified as the People's Republic of China) in connection with a KYTC project supported by Federal Highway Administration funds
requirement_type: Prohibition (as a condition of using federal funds), flowing down from KYTC to its consultants and contractors
permit_or_approval_required: No permit process; compliance is a contract/funding condition, with exemptions and waiver procedures reserved to federal agencies under the American Security Drone Act framework

summary: KYTC's Department of Aviation serves as the Executive Branch's UAS information clearinghouse, primarily directing operators to FAA registration, Part 107 certification, TRUST testing, LAANC, Remote ID, and B4UFLY resources rather than imposing independent state-level operating rules. Separately, a December 19, 2025 KYTC Design & Construction Memorandum (CM 25-09 & DM 06-25), transmitting an FHWA Kentucky Division notice and the underlying OMB Memorandum M-26-02 (November 21, 2025), notifies KYTC districts, offices, and "active consultants and highway contractors" that, effective December 22, 2025, federal funds (including grants, loans, and cooperative agreements) may not be used to procure, operate, or maintain a UAS — including its flight controller, camera, or ground control station — manufactured by or subject to the control of a foreign-adversary country, specifically identified as the People's Republic of China. "Industry partners" are defined to include any company performing federally funded Cabinet work, expressly including planning studies, design, surveying and imagery, construction engineering, and inspection. The memorandum directs recipients to stop pending procurements of covered equipment, cease operating/maintaining/processing data from existing covered UAS on FHWA-funded work, and physically segregate such equipment to prevent inadvertent use on federally funded projects.

summary: No Kentucky Governor executive order, Kentucky Attorney General opinion, or Kentucky state-court (trial or appellate) decision directly and dispositively addressing UAS regulation was located in this research pass. The one federal court decision arising from a Kentucky UAS dispute, Boggs v. Merideth, No. 3:16-CV-00006 (W.D. Ky. 2017) (the "drone slayer" case, following William Merideth's 2015 shootdown of a neighbor's drone), was dismissed for lack of federal subject-matter jurisdiction; the court expressly declined to resolve the underlying substantive question of whether a drone operator flying at low altitude over private property is in "navigable airspace" versus trespassing on the property below, holding only that the plaintiff's declaratory-judgment and trespass-to-chattels claims did not raise a substantial federal question. No Kentucky statute imposing a state/local-government UAS procurement restriction tied to a "country of concern" or "foreign principal" (of the kind enacted in some other states) was located; the closest analogous restriction identified is the federal American Security Drone Act/OMB M-26-02 framework that KYTC has begun implementing for its own federally funded work (KY-007), not an independent Kentucky statute. No statewide statute expressly preempting local UAS ordinances was located; secondary sources report that most Kentucky municipalities have not adopted their own drone ordinances, with Bowling Green's city parks department cited as an example of a local government imposing its own drone-related permission requirement, but confirming and cataloguing any such local ordinance is out of scope for this state-level phase.

notes: MATERIAL FINDING FOR SITUATIONAL AWARENESS: Boggs v. Merideth is frequently cited by secondary drone-law sources as having "decided" that drone flights over private property are lawful, or conversely that shooting down a trespassing drone is lawful; per the Butler Weihmuller Katz Craig LLP summary reviewed, the court did neither — it dismissed for lack of federal subject-matter jurisdiction without reaching the merits of either the airspace-trespass question or the shootdown's lawfulness. AEC firms should not treat this case as having established a Kentucky legal rule on low-altitude UAS property rights; the question remains open under Kentucky law. Also note for currency tracking: KRS 500.130's 2025 amendment (KY-001) created a new private civil cause of action under new sections of KRS Chapters 411 and 413 for the surveillance-recording prohibition, a different, statutorily created remedy from the common-law trespass-to-chattels theory at issue in Boggs.
